sections: Asks whether a machine that broadly exceeds human intelligence could design a stronger successor.
Treats machine design as an intellectual activity whose improvement could feed back into later design.
A conditional argument about intelligence and design, rather than an estimated growth model or sufficient-condition theorem.
Discusses parallel computation, meaning and human–machine cooperation without supplying an engineering blueprint.
Envisages acquiring equipment and improving designs; no implemented generation, evaluation and inheritance experiment.
A historical formulation of the research question. Intelligence explosion is the hypothesis under discussion, not an experimentally established law.
Studies discovery of concepts and heuristics that influence subsequent exploration.
Represents knowledge and heuristics through common units and slots, including provenance, value and applicability.
Allocates work through topic, task and rule agendas; Select–Execute–PostMortem updates heuristic value using results and costs.
Combines, generalizes and specializes knowledge. Domain representations and initial rules remain human-designed.
Useful heuristics enter later search. Although the representation allowed control modification, reported attempts at changing the main controller produced bugs.
A precursor to inherited meta-heuristics and computational allocation, with domain demonstrations rather than modern matched-budget transfer evidence.
Formalizes when a program should rewrite itself by proving an expected-utility benefit.
A proposed switch must outperform continued proof search, accounting for the opportunity cost of waiting.
Axioms describe hardware, software, environment assumptions and utility; a proof searcher seeks a justified switch program.
The initial searcher and other program components can be rewritten, subject to proofs in the fixed formal system.
Successors can continue self-modification. Beneficial changes need not be discoverable or provable within a useful time.
A formal reference point for self-modification. Its conditional optimality depends on axioms and utility; it is not an implemented LLM result.
Learns rapid adaptation to new tasks from few examples and gradient steps.
Optimizes performance after adaptation, producing an initialization that responds effectively to task data.
An inner update uses support examples; the outer update uses separate query examples and differentiates through adaptation.
Studies full second-order gradients and first-order approximations in regression, few-shot classification and reinforcement learning.
Initialization parameters accumulate across tasks; adaptation uses a researcher-specified update procedure.
Establishes a reusable bilevel-learning template. It does not recursively rewrite learner code or establish adaptation to arbitrary task distributions.
Learns strong Go play from rules and random initialization without human game records.
Search improves action targets; the network compresses and generalizes the search results.
One network predicts moves and outcomes; MCTS supplies policy targets and self-play outcomes supply value targets.

The three-day experiment generated about 4.9 million games with 1,600 simulations per move. Candidate replacement required over 55% wins in 400 games; four TPUs describe playing configuration, not total training cost.
Weights and generated games change between rounds, while Go rules, MCTS and training algorithms remain fixed.
Reported a 100–0 match against AlphaGo Lee. Demonstrates search–learning feedback in a precisely specified domain, rather than unrestricted open-world recursion.
Searches for learning algorithms with fewer supplied machine-learning primitives.
Makes Setup, Predict and Learn programs editable sequences of elementary mathematical instructions.
Programs operate on scalar, vector and matrix memory; a fixed evolutionary algorithm selects them by validation performance.
Mutates instructions through insertion, deletion and replacement, using proxy tasks and later larger-input or new-dataset evaluation.
Successful learning programs enter later populations; the outer evolutionary search procedure remains fixed.
Rediscovered backpropagation-like structures and useful combinations. Conclusions depend on the instruction space, proxy tasks and search budget.
Treats the program improver itself as a program that can be improved by self-application.
Defines meta-utility by the quality of downstream programs produced by a candidate improver, without exposing the concrete evaluation tasks directly in its self-edit prompt.
The current improver edits its own search, prompting, selection and budget logic; the LLM, external utility and resource limits stay fixed.

GPT-4-0314 experiments used 20 noisy-parity instances for candidate evaluation and 50 independent instances for reporting across five runs. A selected successor transferred to five tasks; reported 3SAT utility rose from 21.2% to 75.1%.
Executable improvers are inherited. GPT-3.5 and Mixtral controls degraded overall; individual runs were non-monotonic, and utility implementation defects could be exploited.
Provides a clear self-application interface and finite-round transfer evidence for frozen-model program improvement. Improving task optimization does not automatically preserve self-editing ability.
Addresses prompt search that stagnates when its mutation instructions never change.
Evolves task prompts together with mutation prompts and optional successful demonstrations.
Tournament selection and nine operators generate task-prompt variants, mutate mutation instructions, induce prompts from solutions and perform crossover. PaLM 2-L and the outer search stay fixed.
Typical runs use 50 individuals, 20–30 generations and 100 training examples per fitness estimate. Reported GSM8K zero-shot performance is 83.9%, versus 77.9% for APE in the table.
Prompts, mutation prompts and examples are inherited. An ETHOS ablation reduced 81.6% to 64.6% when removing induction from correct solutions in the reported reduced-budget setting.

Demonstrates coupled prompt and mutation-strategy evolution. Cross-domain applicability of the search algorithm is different from transfer of a single evolved improver; some comparison baselines use different models.
Uses language-generated programs and executable feedback to find mathematical constructions and algorithms.
Retains short generating programs so discovered structures can be interpreted and reused.
A frozen LLM proposes programs from an island-organized database; execution supplies scores and population diversity supports exploration.
Researchers provide a program skeleton and evaluator; the model edits a priority function. Low-performing islands are periodically reset.
Problem-solving programs persist, while the FunSearch sampling and improvement machinery remains fixed.
Reported an eight-dimensional cap set of size 512, found in four of 140 experiments, and further results involving human analysis. The improved object is the external solution program.
Uses the current model's errors to extract more learning signal from an existing demonstration dataset.
Treats demonstrations as positive examples and model-generated responses as changing negative examples.
Each round optimizes logistic differences of policy-to-reference log ratios. Fixed-point results assume an expressive model class and idealized optimization.
Zephyr-7B-SFT experiments use 50,000 prompts; later rounds combine old and fresh negatives into 100,000 pairs. Six-task Open LLM averages rise from 58.14 to 63.16 and MT-Bench from 5.94 to 6.78.
Updated parameters become the next generator and reference. Demonstrations and the training rule remain fixed; refreshing negatives outperforms additional training on stale ones in the ablations.
Shows the value of adaptive contrastive data. The existing UltraChat demonstrations still provide the target distribution, and gains diminish across the reported rounds.
Studies whether one model can improve both answering and judgment while generating its subsequent preference data.
Treats evaluation as instruction following, allowing shared parameters to influence both responses and future feedback.
Llama 2 70B receives instruction and evaluation SFT, then two rounds of self-scored preference generation and DPO. A fixed 0–5 rubric selects highest-versus-lowest pairs.
Four answers per prompt are each scored three times; the rounds produce 3,964 and 6,942 pairs. A frozen Llama 2-Chat 70B generates prompts, and Claude 2 assists validation-based early stopping.
Weights pass from M1 to M2 to M3. Held-out human-preference agreement rises from 78.7% to 80.4% and 81.7% without new evaluation fine-tuning data.
AlpacaEval 2 wins against GPT-4-Turbo rise from 9.94% to 15.38% and 20.44%. Output length also grows; this is a finite shared-role feedback result, not a general guarantee of better judging.
Lets an agent inspect and edit both its task-solving code and its improvement logic.
Places introspection, code modification and environment interaction in one action space; edits can change algorithms rather than only prompts.
Monkey patching replaces functions, classes and variables at runtime. The objective, external model service and task evaluator remain supplied by the experiment.
Six optimization runs per task use up to 30 rounds. Restricted GPT-3.5 experiments report MGSM 53.4%→64.2% and DROP 79.4→80.9; unrestricted results partly benefit from calling GPT-4o.
Modified logic continues execution. Among 100 MGSM runs, 92% temporarily declined, 4% terminated unexpectedly and 14% ended below the starting policy.
Demonstrates executable self-modification, including enumeration for Game of 24. Cross-successor transfer of improvement ability and weight learning are not established by these experiments.
Automates discovery of agent prompts, control flow and collaboration in a program search space.
Code represents conditions and loops; an archive preserves earlier designs as reusable stepping stones.
A fixed meta-agent writes a forward function, reflects on novelty and correctness, repairs execution errors and adds evaluated programs to the archive.
Uses 25 search rounds for ARC and 30 for other domains. GPT-4 designs and GPT-3.5 executes in the main setup; reported best DROP and MGSM scores are 79.4 F1 and 53.4%.
Programs and their evaluation records persist; the meta-agent and outer loop are fixed. Transfer experiments reuse structures across models and related tasks.
Provides evidence for automated agent architecture search. Reported discovery and evaluation costs are about $500 for ARC and $300 for other domains; these are separate from deployment cost.
Organizes workflow optimization as a search tree to use prior modifications and failures efficiently.
A search-tree node is a complete workflow; nodes inside that workflow are model calls. Reusable operators supply structural priors.
A modified MCTS selects parent workflows, an LLM edits prompts or code, and repeated validation sends results back to the search history.

Six datasets use a 1:4 validation/test split and up to 20 search rounds, with five evaluations per candidate. The reported average is 80.3 across heterogeneous metrics versus 76.0 for CoT-SC and 67.2 for ADAS.
Workflow code and parent-linked experience persist. Removing predefined operators still reaches 93.1% on GSM8K in the reported ablation; cross-model transfer varies.
A fixed optimizer improves executable workflows and deployment cost–quality trade-offs. The mixed-metric average is not one success rate, and deployment cost does not measure total discovery cost.
Runs improvement of the coding agent as a coding task, with the best archived agent developing its successor.
Targets editing, navigation, context management and subagent coordination; reported changes include differential editing, AST navigation and context summaries.
Editable agent code is scored by performance, cost and latency with weights 0.5/0.25/0.25. The evaluation and selection loop is fixed; tasks time out at 300 seconds and the cost term caps at $10.

Uses 50-task SWE-bench Verified and LiveCodeBench subsets plus synthetic editing/navigation tasks, mainly with Sonnet 3.5 v2 and an o3-mini reasoning subagent. SWE subset performance reaches 53% from 17%, with 51% at round 15.
Source, utility and runs enter an archive. Some navigation data had dependency defects; gains on LiveCodeBench were smaller, and AIME/GPQA often relied on the stronger reasoning subagent.

Shows inherited full-harness modification under several resource objectives. The SWE number is not the full 500-task result, and fixed-set selection leaves independent transfer as a separate question.
Preserves diverse self-modifying coding agents so temporarily weaker versions can become useful stepping stones.
Selects parents using performance and descendant history, retaining multiple lineages rather than only the current champion.
Agents inspect failures and edit their tools, prompts, context and control code. Foundation weights, archive management and parent-selection rules stay fixed in the main experiment.
Runs 80 search rounds per coding benchmark. SWE 20%→50% concerns a hierarchical subset of up to 200 tasks; Polyglot is 14%→38% on the search subset and 14.2%→30.7% on the full benchmark.
Fixed-meta-agent and no-archive controls perform worse. A SWE-evolved agent reaches 28.9% on Polyglot unused in search, compared with the initial 14.2%.
Supports inherited, transferable harness changes. An appendix estimates about $22,000 per SWE search versus roughly $10,000 for baselines; stronger successors can also cost more at inference.
Extracts actionable improvement information from trajectories and textual execution feedback rather than only scalar rewards.
Uses reflection to localize failures and Pareto selection to retain candidates that excel on different examples.
A fixed optimizer selects a prompt module, executes a minibatch, proposes an edit and evaluates promising candidates; optional merging combines complementary modules.
Six benchmarks use Qwen3-8B and GPT-4.1-mini. An IFBench example reaches 38.61% with 678 rollouts versus GRPO's 35.88% with 24,000; AIME is a counterexample to universal superiority over RL.

Prompts, lineages and per-example scores persist. Pareto selection helps in ablations; merging helps one model but can hurt another. Training-feedback, selection and final-test sets have separate roles.
A sample-efficient reflective prompt optimizer, not a self-replacing optimizer. Rollout counts exclude differences in reflection compute; appendix GPT-4.1-mini GEPA experiments cost about $86.
Searches multi-agent scaffolds to study how organization changes capability and behavioral trade-offs.
Maintains structural diversity through code-description clustering and Pareto candidates within clusters.
Starts from seven human-designed scaffolds. Fixed Claude 3.5 Sonnet mutates and crosses programs executed by GPT-4o-mini; operators and the outer algorithm do not evolve.
Single- and dual-objective experiments use 20 generations with ten variants per generation. Reported single-objective DROP is 72.3 F1 and GPQA 41.2%, with modest gains over existing structures.
Scaffolds, clusters and Pareto fronts persist. A refusal-heavy candidate scores 95.2% on SaladData but only 49.6% helpfulness on TruthfulQA, exposing objective substitution.
Provides automated structural search and multi-objective comparisons. Discovered scaffolds do not replace the meta-agent, and small score differences do not establish broad recursive improvement.
Studies learnability when a system can adaptively modify its hypothesis class.
The relevant statistical object is the union of prediction functions reachable by all allowed modifications.
Under binary classification, 0–1 loss, IID sampling and measurability conditions, finite VC dimension of the reachable envelope characterizes distribution-free PAC learnability.
A Two-Gate rule requires membership in a predetermined capacity envelope and validation improvement above an estimation-error threshold.
Repeated validation use is justified only under the fixed-envelope and threshold assumptions; self-modifying controllers must preserve these invariants.
Clarifies adaptive search and validation reuse. The terminal bound compares against the best member of the terminal class, not every reachable program or an arbitrary practical search algorithm.
Learns how to turn new information into useful parameter updates rather than only answering the current question.
Self-edits contain synthetic knowledge text or augmentation and fine-tuning instructions; their value depends on the learner they adapt.

An outer model generates edits, an inner SFT update produces an adapted model, and downstream performance scores the edits. ReST-EM-style filtering and cloning avoid differentiating through the entire inner training loop.

Qwen2.5-7B no-context SQuAD improves from 33.5% using raw-text adaptation to 47.0%; joint adaptation over 200 articles reaches 43.8%. ARC uses a 1B model and eight selected test tasks; 72.5% refers to edit configurations.
The knowledge branch uses two outer rounds, 50 articles per round, five edits per article and three inner adaptations per edit. Sequential edits reveal forgetting.
Makes learning-to-adapt executable and reports transfer to multi-document adaptation. Evaluation requires actual inner training, about six hours per round on two H100s in the reported setup.
Jointly edits task-agent and meta-agent code to study improvement capability beyond coding-task performance.
Measures imp@k: the best task-agent gain produced by a fixed meta-agent within k modification attempts.

Task and meta code evolve in a DGM-style archive; foundation weights, parent selection and evaluation remain fixed in the main experiment. Robot-policy training is distinct from training the foundation LLM.

Tests coding, paper-acceptance judgments and robot reward design, with Olympiad grading as a transfer task. Transferred programs obtain median imp@50 of 0.63 across five runs, while the initial meta-agent is near zero.

Both task and meta programs transfer, and the initial grading baseline includes formatting failures. At 200 rounds, 0.64 versus 0.61 is not significant; a ProofAutoGrader-based experiment improves full-benchmark accuracy from 0.561 to 0.601.
Provides direct improvement-budget measurements and cross-domain experiments. Short-budget adaptation gains are stronger evidence than the reported long-run compounding comparison.
Separates the ability to write a useful harness from the ability to benefit from one.
Crosses solver and evolver models so improvement quality and execution compatibility can be compared separately.
Weights stay frozen. SWE and SkillsBench update skills; MCP-Atlas also permits prompts and appended memory. Benefit is the best observed gain among three evolvers, not a theoretical optimum.
Uses 500 SWE-bench Verified, 500 MCP-Atlas and 86 SkillsBench tasks in an online task stream; anonymized trajectories receive fixed-model adherence judgments.
Skills and memories persist across tasks while the update algorithm stays fixed. This is online adaptation, not a separate final-harness test on a new task distribution.
Average evolver gaps on three anchor solvers are at most 3.1 percentage points, and a 9B evolver sometimes matches larger models. Loading and actually following skills are distinct bottlenecks.
Combines harness edits and target-model training to address failures that either intervention alone may leave unresolved.
A fixed Claude Sonnet 4.6 feedback agent inspects trajectories and chooses whether to change programs or train the gpt-oss-120b target.
Harness steps freeze weights; training steps freeze the harness and update rank-32 LoRA. The demonstrated tasks generally search harnesses first and train after progress stalls.

LawBench uses PPO/GAE, GPU kernels entropic advantages and single-cell denoising GRPO. Reported harness-only versus joint results include 50.0%→70.1% on LawBench and 0.241→0.289 normalized denoising reconstruction.
Programs, execution experience and target adapters persist; the feedback model and task verifier remain fixed.

Demonstrates target-model/harness joint optimization. The legal setup explicitly uses the test split to supply training reward, so its 70.1% is benchmark-feedback optimization rather than independent held-out generalization.
Adapts task-specific multi-agent organization around a fixed coding model.
Uses adjacent-version preference comparisons and explicit communication contracts to reduce redundant shared context.
A fixed agent executes a text harness; a fixed judge compares artifacts; a fixed optimizer revises roles, instructions, hops and termination using preference history.

Thirty synthetic ML-research tasks cover finance, robotics and drugs. After two rounds, Sonnet wins 20 of 30 comparisons against the max baseline; judgments inspect designated deliverables rather than reproducing all research.
Text harnesses and comparisons persist. An Opus run costs 1.69 normalized units versus 2.19 for max and 4.15 for ultracode; these exclude earlier search costs.
Supports limited-round, task-specific coordination adaptation. It does not independently demonstrate unseen-task transfer or replacement of the improvement procedure.
Compares harness evolution with repeated sampling and answer revision under explicit budgets and feedback access.
Separates reusable cross-task evolution from adaptation within one task.
Contrasts fixed-harness parallel sampling, sequential revision, cross-task evolution and task-specific scaling, keeping foundation weights fixed.
Terminal-Bench 2.1 uses 89 tasks, three frontier models, K=5 and two runs; a separate 45/10/34 split tests transfer. External retrieval from a prior evolution implementation is disabled.
Long-horizon game experiments instead use continuing environment feedback: 2,000 ARC-AGI-3 actions or 12 EdgeBench hours, with periodic updates.
Terminal held-out mean remains 63.2. In ARC, full-harness adaptation raises reported RHAE from 43.3 to 77.5 for Opus and 21.1 to 38.2 for GPT-5.6 Terra; task structure determines where gains appear.
Alternates repairs to a tool-using math harness with learning from the resulting successful trajectories.
A HarnessCritic distinguishes prompt, schema, skill, middleware and memory failures from errors attributable to the model itself.
With weights fixed, candidates target repeated failures and are checked for regressions; with the accepted harness fixed, fresh verified trajectories supply SFT for the next round.

Qwen3-8B and 32B undergo two joint rounds with five harness steps each. Reported mean accuracy rises from the already harness-optimized R0 value of 58.5% to 78.9%; 32B HMMT25 rises from 49.8% to 77.0%.
Weights and harnesses persist together. A separate 200-hour, 22-version engineering case covers startup repair, batching and rollback; it is not 200 hours of continuous weight training.

Provides an actionable repair-and-internalization loop. Missing training/split details and incomplete matched-cost controls limit attribution; the reported 3.78h-to-1.11h change is not an 8.7-fold reduction.
Builds infrastructure for harness composition and for exporting its successes and failures as future training data.
Pairs sibling trajectories from the same model and task under different harness interventions, preserving the identity of each change.
Composable sessions, hooks, prompts, tools and acceptance interfaces compile into traceable recipes with lockfiles and execution records.

Tests 65 Pi-centered candidates with fixed MiniMax-M2.7-highspeed on 100 AtCoder repair tasks: 6,500 slots scored on public tests. Pi solves 50, the best fixed candidate 52, and the retrospective union 79.
Programs and paired records persist. Follow-ups change repetition and benchmark protocols; no new model is trained and used to rebuild the next harness generation.
Contributes composition and trajectory data engineering. The 79-task oracle union is not the success rate of one deployable system, and the proposed model–harness loop remains unexecuted.
Separates a task harness, an evolver editing it and a meta-evolver editing the evolver's strategy.
Makes the editable boundary explicit: task code and selection/modification strategy can change, while the meta execution template remains fixed.
A shared frozen model uses separate histories and react primitives; versions and experiment notes guide hypotheses, edits, evaluation and selection.

DeepSeek-V4-Flash runs five rounds of at most 80 react steps, with extended reasoning used for improvement but disabled for task execution. Most BALROG tests vary seeds; BabaIsAI also holds out tasks.

Code and evolver strategies persist. BabaIsAI results show strong harness improvement but mixed extra benefit from meta-evolution; navigation changes expose inventory, maps, goals and BFS paths more effectively.
Demonstrates bounded joint evolution of task execution and search strategy. Difficult NLE tasks improve less, and task-family transfer does not establish general improvement-policy transfer.
Trains agents to choose when to use external state rather than always loading all available memory.
Separates Belief, Progress and Experience, making memory operations compete with environment actions for interaction budget.
Qwen3-4B/8B receive teacher-trajectory SFT and GRPO with task, efficiency and annealed coverage rewards. Fixed Claude Opus 4.6 teaches and curates experience in the main setup.
The 8B results are 95.0% ALFWorld, 80.6% WebShop success and 26.0% WebArena, versus 66.4%, 73.0% and 18.0% for ordinary GRPO. Component and reward ablations are reported.
Policy weights and experience content change; harness interfaces remain fixed. Trained-policy evaluation freezes the experience bank, unlike the frozen-model baseline's across-test-task updates.
Shows policy–memory co-adaptation. It is not evidence of runtime-code self-rewriting; its theoretical results rely on optimization assumptions.
Studies whether apparent improvement arises from modifications to execution, evaluation or reporting rather than better task behavior.
Classifies defects by functional location and by the requirement they violate.
Injects paired malicious and benign changes into real code diffs, matching location and surface function; tasks classify snippets or locate changes in full diffs.
The test set contains 1,765 classification and 1,801 localization examples. A GPT-5.6 Luna localizer reports 74.9% recall and 6.3% false positives on benign controls.
Lineage analysis tracks whether flagged changes survive into selected descendants; some early DGM and HyperAgents findings persist.
Makes inherited evaluation defects observable. Real-run percentages are model flag rates rather than fully human-confirmed incidence, and synthetic injections constrain generalization.
Measures whether a creator can develop a reusable executable harness, separating creation from evolution and creator from executor.
Creation begins with an interface/logging seed; behavior is scored from working directories and environment state rather than self-reported completion.
Created artifacts are frozen before execution. Self-Eval shares creator/executor identity; Unified-Eval uses Gemini 3.1 Pro. Development still runs in Claude Code or Codex.
Creation spans five benchmarks and 2,207 instances, with three harnesses per creator–benchmark pair. Coding evolution uses feedback tasks and a separate 630-task SWE holdout.
Across nine lineages and 64 switches, feedback and holdout move together in 34 cases; only two final selections are holdout-best. Many score changes are within rerun noise.

Separates development skill, executor compatibility and selection error. The generated harness does not take over the next development environment; one evolution trajectory per cell limits stable rankings.
Addresses harness search that grows complexity and feedback-set scores without transferable benefit.
Constrains proposal breadth and candidate acceptance, recording failed hypotheses and requiring extra computation to earn useful gains.
A fixed proposer edits open harness components; a fixed critic checks changes; stability and cost rules determine inheritance. L0/L1/L2 names are engineering analogies.
Eight benchmarks cover coding, workspaces and design. Frozen Opus 4.8 results include Terminal 74.2→80.2, unused-in-search SWE-Verified 82.0→83.8 and workspace OOD 39.7→43.6.
Without acceptance rules, OOD falls to 41.0 and tokens rise to 3.59M, versus 43.6 and 2.42M. The original harness uses 1.56M, so regularization limits growth rather than making all runs cheaper.
Provides held-out, cross-benchmark and cross-model evidence for regularized harness optimization. The fixed outer rules do not isolate a successor becoming a stronger improver.
Optimizes complete harness code using a searchable filesystem of source, scores and execution traces.
Lets a coding proposer retrieve detailed history on demand instead of compressing everything into a short context summary.
Fixed Claude Code/Opus 4.6 proposes, checks, executes and records changes to retrieval, memory, context and control; the proposer itself is not replaced.

Covers online classification, retrieval-assisted mathematics and TerminalBench. Math search uses 250 problems, 40 rounds and 109 candidates, then transfers one selected design to 200 unseen problems and other models.
Math transfer averages +4.7 points over no retrieval and +1.3 over BM25. Terminal search and final evaluation share 89 tasks, unlike the independent classification/math designs.
Shows the value of detailed execution history for discovering persistent harnesses. Transfer claims must be read per experiment; Meta does not by itself mean optimizer self-evolution.
Optimizes reusable AI-research search and memory procedures under a fixed task budget.
Separates inner public proxy feedback from outer private scores of submitted solutions across tasks.
A fixed AIDE-human outer researcher edits the inner agent. AIDE85 uses UCB1 over five drafting strategies, periodic cross-strategy restarts, compact history and recurring-error signatures.

An eight-day, 100-node run accepts seven edits and improves private selection score from 0.703 to 0.778, versus a 0.749 human-developed baseline. External ALE, MLE, FML and WeatherBench tests show useful but non-monotonic transfer.
A separate ignition test compares AIDE47 and AIDE-human as outer improvers on the same starting agent over three seeds and 50 rounds; final means 0.780 and 0.782 are inconclusive.
Supports transferable research-harness efficiency. It does not establish acceleration from successor takeover; one proposed selection penalty is reported to leave candidate ordering unchanged.
Frontis-MA1/OpenMLE trains ML-program improvement through executable tasks and combines it with long-horizon search.
Uses Draft, Improve, Debug and Crossover as common operations, reducing dependence of training on one complete controller.
OpenMLE-Gym supplies 5,758 filtered tasks; 26,259 execution-filtered samples precede RL. Adaptive reward normalization, entropic advantages and asynchronous queues support learning.
Full-parameter training starts from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, with a 30B replication. At fixed Evo, MLE-Bench Lite medal rate rises 39.39%→60.61%; adding Evo-Max reaches 71.21%.

Training changes the editing model; deployment inherits candidate programs and structured experience. The paper states that evolution mainly modifies external ML solutions while the evolution system stays largely fixed.

On ten NatureBench Lite tasks, model and search changes have separate benefits. The 12-hour, 12GB-limited RTX 4090 task sandbox excludes model serving and training compute; this is supporting AI4AI work, not completed autonomous joint RSI.
Studies whether coordinated copies of one model can generate better learning experience for that model without a stronger external teacher.
Optimizes role instructions, information handoffs, output contracts and coordination while retaining the underlying qwen-code tools and runtime.

An inner loop compares and revises workflows at fixed weights. An outer loop ranks repeated trajectories through pairwise judgments and Bradley–Terry scores, removes workflow prompts and performs SFT.

Qwen3.6-27B completes two rounds. Round one uses 119 trajectories from eight synthetic tasks and 17.2M stored supervision tokens; rank-64 LoRA training takes about 19 hours on six H100s, excluding collection and search.
The new model takes over execution, optimization and evaluation. Its workflows, executed by the old model, win 64% against old-model workflows; agreement with an external judge rises from 73% to 93%.

After two rounds ScienceAgentBench rises 28.8→31.7 and MLR-Bench 1.58→2.40, while Terminal and SWE scores decline. This is a finite joint-evolution result with measured regressions and unmatched collection costs.
Connects consequence prediction, action selection and real feedback across coding, GUI and scientific applications.
Separates changing task state from inheriting a changed policy, workflow or predictive model.
Candidate actions pass validity and budget checks; feedback updates selected components, followed by component and combination evaluation. Different applications activate different paths.
Coding fixes a 7B solver and adapts a 3B LoRA execution predictor on 200 CodeContests tasks over three seeds. Success is 31.2% versus 29.2% with a fixed world model and 26.3% with a static verifier.
GUI experiments update policy and predictor; laboratory planning tracks five 4B policy versions. Chemistry uses measurements for experiment selection, while the immunology predictor is fixed.
Evidence must be read per application. The paper calls for sustained joint experiments on the same task; small trained components and a 35B comparison model should not be conflated.
Reduces the cost of evaluating research exploration strategies by replaying prior discovery trees.
Reuses observed experimental outcomes rather than inventing unseen results; replay reveals only records along selected paths.
A fixed policy-development agent edits exploration code against historical trees and several budget preferences, then deploys the selected strategy in fresh search.
Covers kernels, mathematics, Lasso and harnesses. Lasso searches 17 synthetic instances and tests six unseen datasets; reported runtime falls 3,587.1→2,931.0ms and discovery calls 550→317.

Search strategies persist while discovery models and the policy developer stay fixed. TerminalBench repeatedly uses all 89 tasks, reaching 0.8090 from 0.7247; a fixed-exploration control is omitted for cost.
Creates a cheap strategy-testing environment from research history. Replay cannot assess unsupported branches, and improvement on historical trees does not guarantee improved future search.
Allocates resources between creating successors and evaluating existing agents, using lineage potential rather than only current scores.
Clade metaproductivity describes the quality of descendants a node may produce; the practical method estimates it from observed subtrees and uses Thompson sampling.
Agents edit themselves, but HGM selection and scheduling remain fixed. Oracle-based theoretical results rely on restrictive reset, cost and terminal-utility assumptions.
At 800 agent–task evaluations, SWE-60 scores are 56.7/53.3/50.0 for HGM/DGM/SICA and Polyglot 30.5/27.1/25.4, under specified expansion and evaluation models.
At 8,000 evaluations, another stronger SWE starting agent rises 53.2%→61.4%. A de-overlapped 207-task SWE-Lite holdout rises 34.8%→40.1%.
Contributes lineage-aware search and fine-grained evaluation scheduling. Empirical estimates do not inherit oracle optimality; allocated CPU-hours and model compute are distinct costs.
Maintains useful long-term context without repeatedly compressing detailed experience into generic summaries.
Separates a trajectory generator, reflector and curator; identified entries receive local deltas and helpful/harmful counts.
Deterministic merging preserves existing playbook entries, while editing and deduplication manage growth. Weights and role definitions remain fixed.
With DeepSeek-V3.1, reported AppWorld averages move from ReAct 42.4 to offline ACE 59.4; online adaptation with offline warmup reaches 59.5. These average different task metrics.
The playbook persists. Ablations support reflection and repeated integration; offline AppWorld adaptation uses 357 rollouts and 9,517 seconds versus GEPA's 1,434 and 53,898 in that setup.
Makes experience maintenance incremental and traceable. Online prediction-before-update and offline held-out testing are different protocols; inaccurate reflection can still accumulate bad memory.
Searches executable algorithms and mathematical constructions, including improvements to AI infrastructure.
Can evolve both a solution and the heuristic that improves earlier solutions, retaining programs, constructions and evaluation history.

Frozen Gemini models generate code diffs; asynchronous evaluators and a diverse multi-objective database select candidates. Meta-prompts can evolve, while the outer controller and model weights remain fixed.

Reports matching prior best constructions in 75% and improving 20% of over 50 math problems, a 48-multiplication complex 4×4 matrix algorithm, 0.7% recovered cluster compute and a kernel speedup associated with roughly 1% lower Gemini training time.
Evaluation cascades and diverse histories support search. Kernel shapes and scheduling workloads include held-out checks; deployment provides additional evidence for infrastructure results.
