Trains a specialized engineer to generate runtime patches scored by downstream agent performance.
Provides lifecycle intervention points rather than restricting edits to system prompts.
Failure packets condition executable overlays; frozen targets rerun task batches to reward eight candidate patches per GRPO group. Only engineer weights update.
A Qwen3.5-9B engineer receives 877 teacher patches then about 1,500 failure packets. Equal-weight target success across three environments rises 44.3→53.6%, versus 46.4% with SFT-only editing.

A later experiment first adapts the target on successful traces, then retrains the engineer, improving 59.2→64.2%. Transfer to unseen target configurations regenerates patches rather than training those target models.
Turns harness-editing skill into an execution-trained model. Fixed overlay interfaces and finite environments define scope; sequential adaptation is not sustained two-way co-evolution.
Abstracts successful and failed trajectories into reusable strategies and trains policies to apply them.
A hierarchical SkillBank separates general planning/recovery principles from task-specific skills produced by a fixed strong teacher.
Qwen2.5-7B receives skill-use SFT and GRPO with retrieved skills; poorly performing categories trigger skill additions and revisions.
Reports ALFWorld 89.9% versus ordinary GRPO 77.6%, WebShop 72.7% versus 66.1%, and transfer across five held-out QA datasets.
Weights and the library change together. Freezing skills lowers results; removing hierarchy or replacing abstractions with raw trajectories degrades further. The bank grows from 55 to 100 skills.
Provides a finite policy–experience-library loop and useful ablations. Teacher and update rules stay fixed; reported RL uses eight H100s for about 24 hours and all students are 7B.
Optimizes compact, transferable skill files against repeated execution with a fixed target model.
A textual learning rate limits edit counts, while successes protect working behavior and rejected edits prevent repeated failed proposals.
An optimizer reflects on minibatches, merges suggestions and edits within budget; selection and final-test sets are separate.
Persistent state includes current/best skills, hashes, rejection records and slower guidance. An optimizer-side meta-skill learns editing patterns but is not deployed with the final skill.
Across 52 measured settings, the paper reports best or tied results; GPT-5.5 direct-call averages rise 58.8→82.3. Removing meta-skill and slow updates substantially harms a spreadsheet configuration.
Shows portable procedural knowledge, including cross-harness spreadsheet transfer. Benefits vary by domain, and training-call cost must be amortized over later use.
Couples persistent experience with expansion of executable tools and expert assets.
Assets encode available actions; experience records when to use them and how to build better assets.
MCP tool code, interfaces and expert specifications are retrieved before creating missing capabilities; experience guides planning, construction and execution.
Model judgments generate critiques; proposed assets must pass critique-derived execution tests and can be repaired. Successes and failures become reusable experience.
GPT-5-chat averages 70.24 pass@1 across eight benchmarks versus Alita 63.78. Experience raises first-test asset validity 53.1→72.4% and lowers repair rounds 1.01→0.48.
Reports transfer of GAIA-derived memory to other tasks. Both evolving objects are in the harness, not foundation weights; generated tests and judges remain imperfect feedback.
Learns how to select and construct memory-processing operations rather than training a larger language model to memorize facts.
Distinguishes stored content from skills for extracting, summarizing and updating it.
A lightweight MLP controller uses PPO for top-k skill selection; fixed Llama 3.3 70B executes skills, while a fixed designer proposes periodic library edits from difficult cases.
LoCoMo uses a 6/2/2 split of ten conversations. Reported judge score is 50.96 versus 45.86 for random selection and 44.11 for static skills; reuse with fixed Qwen3-Next-80B reaches 52.07.
Controller weights, skills and memory persist. ALFWorld results also improve, without training the foundation LLM or its adapters.
A harness-level controller–library learning method. Small dialogue splits and model judging constrain estimates; large executors are not large trained models.
Learns which semantically relevant memories actually help task execution.
Treats retrieval as an action and attaches utility estimates to experience entries.
Similarity retrieves a candidate pool; normalized similarity and Q-values rank it. Injected entries receive terminal-return EMA updates, and summarized new trajectories enter memory.
Studies coding, lifelong agents, ALFWorld and HLE over repeated online epochs, plus frozen-memory transfer to a 30% holdout.
Contents and retrieval values persist; the update rule stays fixed. Relevance thresholds and value weighting matter in ablations.
ALFWorld final-epoch accuracy is 50.7% versus 27.8% without memory; 69.7% cumulative-ever-solved is a different metric. Frozen-memory transfer is 47.9% versus 31.4%.
Combines executable skill creation with learned context control for data-science agents.
Managers and specialists share a model but have different local contexts and action spaces.
Qwen3-8B roles create validated code skills, promote repeated assets to a library and learn explicit compression actions through SFT and multi-role RL.
About 36,000 filtered teacher trajectories precede three SFT epochs and 300 RL steps on four A800s. Four-benchmark mean is 0.424 versus 0.363 for SFT-only.
The library contains 279 skills with 925 calls and reported 69% cross-task reuse. Removing skills or compression weakens results.
Supports shared-policy management of an expanding library. Reported relative gains differ from percentage points; no separate multi-generation takeover test establishes recursive benefit.
Tests whether teacher imitation remains useful after a harness specializes to a student model.
Highlights behavioral compatibility: teacher plans can change the student's distribution without supplying the ability to execute them.
Fixed Gemini evolves harness components; Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B then receives LoRA training on either whole teacher trajectories or local corrections to student-visited failures.
Mean test success rises 29.2→78.0% after harness search, drops to 63.1% with whole-trajectory imitation and reaches 79.7% with local correction.
About 500 training rows supply short LoRA runs. Failure analysis links imitation to more planning errors, with similar behavior in a supplementary Gemma experiment.
A concrete joint-optimization counterexample and correction principle. Only one harness-search/training sequence is measured; later re-search is proposed rather than demonstrated.
Trains a policy to remain effective as industrial skills, tools and business rules change.
Makes semantically equivalent harness variations part of training, reducing dependence on names, order and fixed formatting.
A 35B-A3B policy receives harness-aware SFT, general-task on-policy distillation and harness-aware RL. AI proposes external edits that developers review and release.
Uses 10,000 SFT samples and 4,000 interaction tasks. Reported live-stream quality rises 80.3→94.8, and changed-harness quality 75.4→94.6.
An independent diagnostic/holdout comparison shows identical harness edits reduce errors more for HAT than fixed-harness SFT, connecting training to the ability to exploit later edits.
An industrial human-in-the-loop co-adaptation result. Whole-system A/B and latency measurements do not isolate model versus harness contributions or establish autonomous research recursion.
Builds an interpretable image-editing evaluator from skill rubrics and visual tools around a frozen VLM.
Separates missing evaluation criteria from perceptual failures such as counting, OCR or spatial analysis.
An orchestrator retrieves skills/tools; a frozen subagent gives ordinal scores. Preference errors trigger library creation, revision or deletion.
One hundred human examples split 60/40 for training and selection. Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Gemini configurations evolve separate libraries.
Across 77 iterations the library expands then contracts to seven assets. The selected evaluator subsequently trains a 4B image editor with GRPO.
Qwen evaluator accuracy rises 30.3→45.7; image-editing score rises 3.32→3.52. This is external reward-system optimization followed by training, not a repeated evaluator–editor co-evolution loop.
Learns web policies and transition models to expand experience beyond expensive successful real browsing.
Separates world-model-generated training experience from additional inference-time lookahead.
Two Llama3.3-70B models predict actions and next accessibility trees; real transitions and selected successful trajectories train them with fixed browser interfaces.
After iterative SFT, selected policy/world-model versions generate short synthetic trajectories. WebVoyager rises 32.98→42.49%, or 51.37% with depth-two lookahead.
Parameters and data persist, not browser code. Actual updates are not synchronized every round, and deeper simulated search degrades after depth two.
Reports several transfer tests, sometimes with additional GPT-4o decomposition or judging. Finite web improvements and model-error limits are distinct from indefinite evolution.
Combines online web interaction, failure-driven curricula and retention of useful prior experience.
Task selection and replay must co-adapt: learnable failures guide new tasks while moderate-difficulty successes prevent forgetting.
Actor and value critic learn; a pretrained 8B outcome model scores new tasks; fixed GPT-4o generates feasible task variations. The policy method can use off-policy replay.
After demonstration SFT, eight rounds select 500 tasks each. On 165 test tasks, reported success is 42.4% for 8B, 43.0% for 9B and 49.1% for a genuinely trained 70B model.
Failures feed the next curriculum and successes enter replay. Removing curriculum, replay or KL controls harms learning or retention.
Provides a repeated parameter-learning web loop at multiple scales. Task generator and reward model do not jointly evolve, and the main environment is WebArena's website set.
Co-trains mathematical generation and process evaluation using search-generated experience.
Uses preferences between steps sharing a prefix instead of regressing noisy exact search values.
A policy emits explanations and Python; a 7B process preference model guides MCTS. Reference answers supply final correctness while executable code filters some failures.
Four rounds use 747,000 math questions; a large coder bootstraps round one. The reported 7B MATH 90.0% includes 64 search trajectories.
Each round retrains the policy from its initial base, carrying improvement through generated data and evaluators. Smaller models use final data rather than all running the full loop.
A substantial finite generator–evaluator learning program, with dozens of GPUs for weeks. Actual evolved models are 7B; executable code alone does not prove reasoning correctness.
Bootstraps an independent reward model from a limited preference-label seed.
Changes pseudo-label filtering from obvious comparisons toward informative finer distinctions as the evaluator improves.
Starting with 15% of labels, the RM scores a fixed answer pool, filters pairs and updates with a pairwise loss and LoRA. PPO training follows after the RM is frozen.
An 8B model's HH-RLHF result rises 56.9→68.56 versus 70.45 with full labels; RewardBench rises 59.1→72.3 versus 75.9.
Several self-labeling rounds retain earlier data. A 70B configuration is described without matching main-table quantitative evidence.
Reduces labeling needs empirically. High-confidence accuracy does not by itself prove monotonic full-distribution improvement, and generator–RM feedback is not experimentally closed.
Adapts training-task allocation to the learner's current needs.
Uses mean absolute advantage as a cheap proxy for useful learning signal, treating task categories as nonstationary bandit arms.
An EMA updates category values; softmax selects categories, uniform sampling selects within them, and fixed GRPO updates the model.
Qwen2.5-3B/7B experiments span arithmetic, logic, ARC and math. Benefits are larger on challenging tasks; some easier settings match random curricula.
Model weights and sampling statistics co-adapt, while reward and update formulas remain fixed. Additional optimizers and task partitions test portability.
Contributes a lightweight adaptive sampler. Absolute advantage omits gradient direction and transfer value, so it is a proxy rather than a guarantee of optimal future generalization.
Explores websites before downstream tasks and turns reusable workflows into Python APIs.
Parameterized, composable skills raise action granularity and can support further skill discovery.
Exploration reads screenshots, URLs and accessibility trees; generated Playwright functions receive documentation, static checks, test inputs and iterative repair.
GPT-4o runs 160 exploration/honing rounds per site. Evaluation covers five WebArena sites, four real sites and reuse by GPT-4o-mini.
APIs persist across tasks and models. The appendix records cases where suppressing an exception was mistaken for fixing semantic behavior.
Reported WebArena means rise 22.6→29.8% for GPT-4o and 9.2→14.1% for mini; real-site mean rises 40.2→56.2%. The discovery and verification procedures themselves stay fixed.
Builds tools on demand while solving a software issue, starting from a minimal bash interface.
Project-specific scripts address bottlenecks discovered during actual execution rather than requiring a complete predefined toolbox.
The model writes, runs and revises tool files within its task trajectory; the agent loop, weights and resource limits remain fixed.
Version one uses Claude 4.5 Sonnet, at most 250 steps and $3 per issue, evaluating 500 Verified and 731 Pro tasks.
Task-local scripts can be reused during the issue. A 50-task ablation scores 62% without creation, 64% with an initial suggestion and 76% with repeated reflection; weaker models can regress.
Reports 75.4% Verified and 45.8% Pro. Evidence concerns task-time tool adaptation, not a persistent cross-task skill library or evolving improver.
Shares experience across evolutionary branches instead of restricting inheritance to one parent lineage.
Selects groups using performance and behavioral novelty measured by task-success vectors.
Two parents exchange framework patches, failures and tool/test feedback; reflection proposes changes and executable descendants enter an archive.
SWE uses staged evaluation; Polyglot separates ten evolution tasks from fifty tests. Model changes occur during search, and the DGM control doubles rounds to match descendant counts.
The best GEA agent incorporates experience from seventeen ancestors versus nine for DGM; injected framework defects are repaired faster in five tests.
Reports SWE 71.0% versus 56.7% and Polyglot 88.3% versus 68.3%, with cross-model reuse. Matched descendants do not match all compute, and model upgrades also affect trajectories.
Maintains reusable capabilities across heterogeneous, changing task streams.
Separates building needed capability from routing each current task to the appropriate existing harness branch.
Analyze, Research, Build and Verify stages use persistent boards, hypotheses and tests. Git preserves specialized branches; feedback arrives when outcomes become available.
Fixed Sonnet solves and Opus evolves across 5,075 PolyBench, 261 CTF and 503 FutureX tasks, with separate autonomous and human-assisted settings.
Research records and branch assets persist. Routing is not uniformly beneficial: a simpler multi-agent FutureX variant scores 49.5% versus 47.3% for the full system.
Reports PolyBench 80.9% and CTF 50.2%. Forecasting backtests are not realized investment returns; limited single trajectories constrain long-term conclusions.
Updates persistent prompts, subagent structure, skills and memory during uninterrupted long games.
A refiner diagnoses recent loops, errors and stalls, treating obsolete external knowledge as a separate source of failure from policy limitations.
After warmup, periodic edits inherit game state. A joint-learning branch collects 256-step windows, filters with a PRM, relabels weak actions with a teacher and performs soft-SFT.
Gemini variants compare minimal, expert and continual harnesses. Gemma training branches include small, 26B and 31B models, but appendix descriptions disagree about the exact online starting model.
Harnesses and game checkpoints persist; some memories are unused and restored checkpoints can temporarily reduce progress.

One 24-hour Flash setting reaches 77% Emerald milestones at about $30, while Flash-Lite edits can underperform a minimal harness. Five joint-learning runs show local progress, not broad monotonic improvement.
Changes training experiences by wrapping existing environments while retaining their original verification.
Stage changes initialization, Contract changes action/observation conditions and Chain composes tasks; transformations can interact.
An EnvRigger diagnoses trajectories, writes and tests wrappers, then distills experiences into ReasoningBank skills for a fixed model. Later rounds target remaining weaknesses.
Across five domains, modified-environment skills improve reported results, including SWE 52.58 versus 49.88; a multi-round environment budget also improves performance.
A separate Qwen3-8B GRPO study supports policy training, with mixed OOD effects. Larger models belong to fixed-model skill experiments, and Chain is not used in the main automatic loop.
Primarily an environment–skill harness method. It assumes suitable resettable interfaces, and equal environment counts do not imply equal total compute.
Evaluates neural architecture composition, operator design and training-script research through execution.
Separates recombination of established modules from discovery of new computational principles.
Fixed models and AIRA-dojo use Draft, Debug, Improve and Analyze; candidate 350M/1B/3B models train and return validation fitness.
Search uses an H200 for 24 hours or 500 steps, longer for larger data; final models use sixteen H200s. A selected 1B composition improves reported validation loss and DCLM scores over its baseline.
Searchers and harnesses stay fixed; trained targets do not take over research. Iterative debugging is essential in low-level design, where one-shot submissions fail.
An AI4AI design benchmark and method study. Researchers use some small-model test scores in later selection, so final large-model downstream tests must be distinguished from that selection stage.
Measures whether research agents can improve AI algorithms through reproducible source changes.
Cleanly reruns submitted source from a fixed start without inheriting exploratory weights or caches.
Ten tasks cover SFT, agentic RL, distillation, reward models, preference optimization, diffusion, unlearning, merging and pruning under fixed final evaluators.
Twenty-nine model/harness/effort configurations create 290 cells, each with four B300 exploration hours and up to twelve validation hours.
Only source crosses into final execution; improved students do not become the next researcher. Code-change categories are model-assisted observational labels.

The normalized mean is 0.166 against a 0.1 original-repository anchor, with 124/290 below baseline. Targets are mostly 1B–7B, and mechanism-changing edits correlate with gains without proving causality.
Provides a common vocabulary for policy iteration, self-modifying programs and mutable evaluators.
Asks which improvement components are editable and what external reference keeps improvement aligned with an objective.
Represents policy, action evaluation, modifier, modification evaluation and grounding, with the agent defined by the chosen editable subset.
Alternating evaluation and improvement plus consistency conditions provide idealized reference structures rather than a complete computable algorithm.
Fixed, mutable or absent grounding yields different feedback regimes; a fixed external judge can still be a biased proxy.
Contributes a comparative formulation and failure questions, not complexity, reachability or general convergence guarantees.
Tests self-improvement from broad goals when an agent must choose data, objectives and validation criteria.
Separates self-chosen proxies from hidden target assessments, distinguishing completing training from retaining useful capability.
Allows either weights or harness edits while holding the other fixed, across six goals and 520 expert-authored projects.
Main weight runs use 4B/9B models, SFT/GRPO/LoRA and forty GPU-hours per final-only run. Harness experiments create one successor and repeat execution.
Rollback makes retained gains nonnegative by construction. Repeated feedback from a hidden slice turns it into adaptive selection information.

Only a small fraction of reported goal/model settings retain gains; three legal successor harnesses underperform Qwen-Agent. Reveals goal-operationalization difficulty rather than impossibility of RSI.
Tests whether external experience influences decisions through its semantic content.
Intervenes separately on raw trajectories, ordering, relevance, summary meaning and formatting.
Frozen models use ExpeL, Dynamic Cheatsheet, ReasoningBank and G-Memory in offline, online and multi-agent configurations.
Evaluations span QA, mathematics and interactive environments, with detailed retrieval and intervention protocols.
Corrupting raw traces often matters more than changing abstracted summaries; attention analysis supplements rather than replaces behavioral intervention evidence.
Shows task-dependent memory use and failures from stale or overgeneral summaries. Insensitivity on knowledge tasks can reflect adequate parametric knowledge, not an absence of learning ability.
Provides reusable program-evolution infrastructure for costly, repetitive search.
Combines parent quality/diversity, adaptive model selection and novelty checks, crediting improvement relative to parent and baseline.
Island archives accept diffs, rewrites and crossover; code embeddings and optional model judgments reject duplicates. A meta-scratchpad summarizes useful modification strategies.
Applications include AIME solver programs and MoE load-balancing losses. The MoE target is roughly 556M total/82M active parameters trained on 2B tokens.
Programs, histories and strategy summaries persist while model weights and the external selection framework remain fixed.
Reports solver transfer across years/models and useful training-loss candidates. Mathematical program search and AI4AI applications remain distinct, each with supplied evaluators and budgets.
Addresses incorrect consensus being reinforced by answer-majority rewards in label-free reasoning.
Combines answer agreement with a learned verifier that can reject some consistent but invalid reasoning.
Shared generator, verifier and correction roles sample answers, verify majority solutions, balance verification labels and train with answer-anchored GRPO.
Uses 1.7B, 3B and 7B models. A 7B four-task first-answer mean rises from TTRL's 41.1 to 43.8, or 45.8 when correction is allowed.
Verifier, filtering and correction ablations support each component; an independent process-reward benchmark also improves.
Provides a mechanism against consensus errors, while shared parameters and pretraining biases still leave no logically independent truth source. Correction adds inference cost.
Learns individual task value for RL post-training rather than relying only on fixed difficulty buckets.
Estimates policy improvement from changes in probabilities of old trajectories after an actor update.
A 0.6B curator selects 256 from 2,048 candidate questions; a 3B actor samples eight answers each, then its estimated gain trains the curator using a clipped bandit-style objective.
Reports the best evaluation within the first 100 steps. Qwen ARC-hard and AIME improve over comparison curricula, while MATH500 is below uniform sampling.
Actor and curator co-adapt with fixed tasks, rewards and actor optimizer. Signal and objective ablations matter; larger candidate pools can destabilize learning.
Connects curricula to downstream policy change. Idealized tabular bounds do not directly prove neural clipped-curator convergence; measured overhead varies by task from about 9.34% to 19.40%.
Synthesizes stateful tool environments and updates tasks from policy failures.
Graph-derived tasks and program-derived tasks cover different workflow structures with explicit state and checking.
Fixed large models mine data, synthesize environments and bootstrap traces; Qwen3-8B/14B are the trained policies. Some rewards are rubric-based judgments, others executable scripts.
The resource contains 1,978 filtered environments, 19,822 tools, 40,000 SFT trajectories and 5,000 RL samples. Two diagnostic rounds improve 14B BFCL and Postgres results.
Tasks, environment assets, diagnostics and weights persist; generators do not become stronger through the reported loop.
Supports environment construction linked to policy learning. An internal τ2-Bench table/prose discrepancy prevents treating both number sets as one result; teachers are not trained targets.
SkillOS trains a curator to maintain a reusable Markdown skill library while the task executor remains frozen. The learning target is whether an edit helps later tasks in a related sequence.
Insert, revise, and delete operations make library maintenance an explicit policy. Delayed task success rewards useful knowledge rather than merely well-written summaries.

An 8B curator edits SkillRepo; BM25 retrieves up to five skills. GRPO combines downstream success, valid operations, a 32B quality judge, and compression. Libraries start empty for each training group; at deployment, curator weights are frozen while the library changes.

On ALFWorld, an 8B executor scores 47.9 without memory, 55.7 with ReasoningBank, and 61.2 with SkillOS; average steps fall from 21.1 to 18.9. Training uses 16 H100s for three days on ALFWorld, five on WebShop, and 2.5 on reasoning.
Grouping dependent tasks matters: removing it reduces ALFWorld to 57.3. Training therefore teaches edits with downstream consequences, rather than isolated memory-writing quality.

The result supports learned skill maintenance. Library resets between groups differ from uninterrupted lifelong coevolution; larger judges and executors have separate roles. The main text and appendix differ on whether the KL coefficient is zero or 0.001.
Socratic-SWE generates software tasks around diagnosed weaknesses, then trains a solver on tasks expected to improve a trusted validation objective.

Difficulty alone is an incomplete curriculum signal. The method compares a generated task's gradient with a validation gradient to estimate whether learning from that task points in a useful direction.

A shared Qwen3.5-9B generator and solver use decomposed GDPO rewards, with a fixed Qwen3.6-27B skill teacher. Gates check format, repository existence, stable execution, and repairability. A Skill Registry directs generation; 100 BeyondSWE validation tasks supply target gradients each round.

Three rounds use 12,000 valid tasks each and eight A100s for about 15 hours per round. SWE-bench rises from 42.6 to 50.4, SWE-bench Pro from 17.24 to 22.85, and Terminal-Bench from 10.11 to 14.61. SWE-bench reaches about 52 by round five and then plateaus.
Removing skills costs 4.2 points; ordinary GRPO costs 1.8. Difficulty-only selection trails by roughly 1.6–3 points. A 9B self-teacher reaches 49.8 against 50.4 with the larger teacher.

The mini-SWE harness stays fixed. Validation data participate in task selection, so this is targeted curriculum learning rather than label-free improvement; finite-sample gradient normalization also limits the theoretical interpretation.
Voyager builds an enduring library of executable Minecraft skills through interaction, using a frozen language model.
Skills are programs that can be retrieved and composed. An automatic curriculum seeks new capabilities, while execution feedback helps repair candidate code.

GPT-4 receives structured state through Mineflayer, retrieves up to five skills, and writes JavaScript. Errors, environment feedback, and a GPT-4 success verifier guide up to four repair attempts per task.

The main evaluation uses 160 prompting iterations across three runs. Voyager acquires a mean of 63 unique items, reported as 3.3 times the comparison, and explores 2.3 times as far; diamond acquisition succeeds in one of three runs.
Successful programs persist in the skill library. New-world transfer clears inventory and tests composition, separating retained code from retained game state.

Four transfer tasks are tested three times, and the no-skill baseline still solves some of them. The evidence concerns reusable external skills under a fixed model, API, and framework; the improvement procedure itself does not evolve.
AgentEvolver combines generated tasks, experience-assisted exploration, and step-level credit to improve agent model weights.
Useful experience can guide rollouts without becoming a permanent deployment prompt. Training removes that assistance so that the resulting behavior must be carried by the model.

A fixed Qwen-Plus generates tasks, Qwen3-235B evaluates, and Qwen-Max assigns step credit; the trained models are 7B and 14B. Half the rollouts receive experience assistance. Selective adjustment of positive advantages handles the mismatch between assisted sampling and unassisted training.

On eight A100s, the 14B model's reported average over eight samples rises from 29.8 to 57.6; self-questioning alone reaches 52.3. AppWorld test-normal is 48.7, distinct from the 59.2 development score.

Process and outcome rewards work best together. Without selective boosting, experience-assisted training can fall below ordinary RL, making distribution correction a substantive part of the mechanism.
The work supports internalizing externally supplied experience. The larger task generators and judges remain fixed; their sizes must not be reported as the size of the model undergoing improvement.
MetaEvolve trains a model to improve programs from evaluation feedback, using a fixed search and training framework.
Program revision is learned as a reusable capability. Synthetic histories expose the model to a sequence of progressively better candidates rather than only final solutions.

About 25,000 code problems are reduced to 6,000 diverse examples. Histories are constructed by sorting static candidates. Qwen3-14B is trained with GRPO using correctness and speed fitness: unsuccessful improvement receives −1, while successful improvement receives a fitness difference.
Seven coding datasets contribute 50 tasks each. The comparison called AlphaEvolve uses OpenEvolve with the same 14B model; it is not Google's deployed AlphaEvolve system.
Reported improvement metrics rise from 42.21 to 59.77 on APPS and 27.01 to 57.70 on AtCoder, but fall from 19.06 to 17.77 on Codeforces. These are improvement measures, not pass rates.

On eight AlgoTune tasks, harmonic-mean speedup rises from 1.392 to 2.045, with regressions on some tasks. The learned reviser operates inside fixed island search; the results do not demonstrate evolution of its own trainer.
SEED distillation uses retrospective skills as privileged training context, then deploys the model without that extra context.
A skill can teach which action is valuable even when it should not remain in the final agent prompt. Distillation transfers that guidance into action selection.

A fixed GLM-5.2 extracts skills for 1,440 seed trajectories used in SFT. Online learning obtains rollouts and skills from a preceding checkpoint, scores actions with and without skills, and combines stop-gradient teacher gating, weighted action likelihood, and GRPO rather than full-distribution KL distillation.
For a 3B model, ALFWorld rises from 75 to 91.8, WebShop from 63.3 to 78.9, and search from 36.4 to 45.7. The 7B model is not best in every setting.

Shared action and analysis weights evolve across rounds; deployment does not retain a growing skill library. On ALFWorld, removing startup training gives 86, removing distillation gives 87, and static skills give 84.4, versus 91.8 for the full method.
This is a concrete route from external experience to model parameters. Teacher scale, trained-model scale, and deployment memory are separate properties of the system.
RL-Tango jointly improves a reasoning generator and a process verifier using final-answer labels to ground their feedback.
A verifier can learn from completed outcomes without requiring human labels for every intermediate reasoning step. The generator then receives finer-grained credit than an outcome alone provides.

A Qwen-Math-7B generator is first supervised with a fixed Llama-70B teacher; a 7B verifier is warmed up before alternating three generator updates with one verifier update. Process rewards use length normalization and decay, while verifier training balances classes.

At a matched 200-step budget, reported math performance rises from 37 to 46.1 and out-of-distribution performance from 57.6 to 61.1. AIME 2025 rises from 10 to 20 under greedy, zero-shot pass@1 evaluation.
Generator and verifier updates form the learned feedback loop. Role-freezing experiments in a toy setting help separate the contribution of each learner.

A Llama-8B experiment improves from 25.1 to 28.8. The 70B teacher remains fixed; it is not the co-trained generator. Final-answer supervision supplies an external anchor for the evolving process reward.
Iterative RPO trains Llama-2-70B-Chat on correctness-ranked reasoning pairs generated by successive checkpoints.
Preference optimization can reinforce relative quality while a positive likelihood term preserves useful complete reasoning. Repeating generation after an update changes the training distribution.
The objective combines DPO with length-normalized likelihood on preferred responses. GSM8K positives also include human gold chain-of-thought, so the feedback is not entirely self-generated.

Greedy GSM8K accuracy progresses from 55.6 to 73.1, 78.0, 81.1, and 81.6; 32-sample voting reaches 88.7. DPO alone gives 61.8 against 73.1 for the first full round; doubling first-round data gives 74.8, below the second round's 78.0.
Sampling temperature changes from 0.8 to 1.3, while available ARC pairs shrink from about 20,000 to 11,000 and 5,000. The pairing and optimization rules stay fixed.

ARC improves from 77.8 to 86.7 and MATH from 12.5 to 20.8, or 29.1 with 32-sample voting. Most benchmarks use separate training runs, so these numbers should not be read as one universally improved checkpoint.
DeepSeekMath-V2 develops natural-language proof generation alongside a verifier and a meta-verifier.
Checking a specific alleged error is often easier than independently finding every error in a proof. Meta-verification therefore targets the quality of verifier critiques.

Expert scores and critique labels train the verifier and meta-verifier with GRPO. Generator reward combines proof quality at weight 0.76 and self-evaluation trust at 0.24. The generator is initialized from a trained verifier; rejection fine-tuning supplies later-round data.

Training draws on 17,503 AoPS problems. Meta-verifier quality rises from 0.85 to 0.96 without a corresponding change in coarse grading accuracy. High-compute inference uses 64 candidates, 64 verifications, and up to 16 refinement rounds.
The last two rounds replace human labels with automatic labels. Expert evaluation reports five of six IMO problems solved and 118/120 on Putnam, under the stated search procedure.

Total training rounds and GPU cost are incompletely reported. Meta-verification checks proposed error claims, not errors the verifier never notices; the competition results describe a search-and-verification system rather than one unassisted answer.
Kimi K2 combines a large mixture-of-experts actor with an evolving critic for reinforcement learning across verifiable and subjective tasks.
Verifiable outcomes can calibrate a critic that also supplies feedback where exact answers are unavailable. This connects objective checks with learned preference judgments.

The model has 1.04 trillion total parameters and 32 billion active parameters. The critic begins with public and internal preference supervision, then receives online verifiable feedback. Actor optimization uses rubric-ranked pairs and a squared log-ratio/advantage objective.

The tool environment includes about 3,000 real MCP tools, 20,000 synthetic tools, stateful interactions, and code execution. Reported tau-bench-2 performance is 66.1 versus 48.8 for DeepSeek; SWE-bench is 65.8 for a single attempt and 71.6 with selection.

Actor and critic can improve together, but a confident critic may still reproduce biased rubrics. The report does not fully disclose critic-update frequency, component ablations, or the complete RL budget.
The 15.5-trillion-token pretraining total is not an RL compute budget. Single-attempt and selected-run scores describe different inference costs and must remain separate.
Large Language Models Can Self-Improve tests whether a model can consolidate the stronger reasoning implicit in multiple samples into more reliable individual responses.

For each question, PaLM-540B generates 32 reasoning paths. Majority answers become pseudo-labels, all rationales supporting that answer are retained, and four combinations of few-shot prompting and chain-of-thought diversify the training format.
This is one offline generate-filter-SFT cycle. Majority voting, templates, and optimization remain fixed; a small set of human reasoning examples and pretrained knowledge provide the starting point.

On GSM8K, single-path accuracy rises from 56.5 to 73.5 and self-consistency from 74.4 to 82.1. Removing chain-of-thought gives 61.6; using only few-shot chain-of-thought gives 69.4, against 73.5 for the full mixture.

One checkpoint trained jointly on six tasks improves on six untrained datasets, including MNLI-m from 72.0 to 81.8. Starting from only ten real questions to synthesize GSM training questions gives 66.2 single-path and 78.1 consensus accuracy, below training with real questions.

The 540B model is actually self-trained; UL2-20B is a smaller replication, while 62B and 8B models receive distilled 540B traces. The work establishes large-scale one-round self-training, with no multi-generation stability experiment.
OPHIS organizes automated experiments around Observation, Problem, Hypothesis, Intervention, and Speed-up, using training dynamics to identify actionable bottlenecks.
Final validation scores identify better candidates but often fail to explain why. Mechanism-oriented observations can direct interventions and reduce uninformative search.

The system examines weights, gradients, activations, and other trajectories, then changes the target training code or configuration. The core is described as non-LLM, while the NanoGPT example explicitly uses a coding agent; these are distinct components.

For grokking, 255 of 350 OPHIS interventions improve substantially and 48 fail; the LLM comparison improves in 44 of 76 executed interventions and fails in 32. Candidate execution and effort differ. NanoGPT uses one H200, 2,000 fixed steps, and ten evaluations per candidate.

Approximately 6,000 observations inform the NanoGPT context, of which about 13% are shown publicly. Repeated measurements and ablations examine both mean gains and unstable variance, but the complete observation-selection and intervention policy is undisclosed.

NanoGPT BPB changes from 0.9340967 to a best candidate of 0.9318420, a difference of 7.43 baseline standard deviations; 376 interventions exceed a three-standard-deviation threshold. These are company-reported results on specific small training problems, not demonstrated self-updates of the research engine.
ComfyResearch is a visual workbench for deep-learning experiments, exposing executable dependencies among data, models, losses, optimizers, training, and analysis.
A typed computational graph makes the intervention explicit: one node can change while its dependencies remain traceable. Configuration, measurements, and model structure retain a common provenance.

The release describes 33 observable-node types, including weights, gradients, Hessians, and rank. Measurements can run during training or on checkpoints; parameter grids expand to at most 256 combinations. An agent can assist with wiring.

Examples include modular-addition grokking, VGG11 mechanics, CIFAR mode connectivity, sharp minima, deep linear models, random labels, and TinyShakespeare rank dynamics. They demonstrate a runnable experimental tool, not a new algorithm in every example.
People inspect curves and choose subsequent experiments. Persistent assets are the graph, configuration, and results; the demonstrated research loop remains human-directed.

Its contribution is observable, reproducible experiment infrastructure. The release does not measure autonomous discovery success or sustained self-improvement; integration with a research agent is an interface opportunity rather than an already validated RSI result.
NanoGPT Observables exposes internal training measurements so researchers can investigate layers and modules beyond a final loss value.
Aggregate norms can hide local behavior. Aligning observations with model structure and controlled variants narrows the hypothesis space, while causal interpretation still requires interventions.

The resource contains 1,820 curves in eight families. The baseline is GPT-2-style NanoGPT with 12 layers, 12 heads, width 768, context 1,024, OpenWebText, AdamW, 2,000 warmup steps, and a cosine schedule recorded through 100,000 steps.

Comparisons use a six-layer model and a 12-layer model without warmup. Users can annotate intervals and combine up to six curves. The highlighted second block's attention entropy moves roughly from 4 to 2 and then 2.5; these are trajectory values, not performance gains.
Humans browse and interpret the measurements. The persistent contribution is a structured observation dataset and annotation interface, rather than an autonomous proposal-evaluate-inherit loop.

The resource enriches feedback for mechanism research. Three training configurations do not establish causal laws or transfer across architectures, scales, and optimizers; those require subsequent controlled experiments.
Apex-Tune reports optimization artifacts across prediction functions, short language-model training, GPU kernels, and attention, with an eight-page report and runnable results repository.

The improvements exploit workload structure: separating long trends from transients, touching only used rows in sparse-embedding backward passes, rearranging TriMul data, and reducing attention rescaling within the benchmark's numerical range.

Visible artifacts show candidate code or symbolic functions evaluated for correctness and performance. The full candidate-generation, rejection, memory, and researcher-update algorithms are not disclosed.

NanoChat uses 300 seconds on a B200 across ten seeds; TriMul checks seven H100 shapes; attention compares head dimensions 64, 128, and 256. The report and current repository differ on some SLDBench baselines and seed aggregates.

Repeated seeds and kernel timings test the artifacts. A bounded error on the supplied attention inputs establishes correctness for that test, not a general guarantee for extreme logits. Complete search cost and component ablations are unavailable.

The current NanoChat ten-seed mean is 0.892792 BPB and best run 0.891762; the report's earlier three-seed mean is 0.892426. Same-machine TriMul improves 1064.9 to 1036.1 μs, while listed K-Search is faster at 1030 μs. Attention reaches 430.7/468.4/451.7 TFLOP/s. These are specific AI-engineering results, not proof of researcher self-evolution.
Apex Research reports 34 end-to-end research projects submitted to the May 2026 ACL ARR review cycle, testing execution from ideas and literature through experiments and papers.

Completed research, external review, and inherited improvement of the research system are separate outcomes. The report provides evidence for the first two; it does not expose a cross-project self-improvement mechanism.
The workflow covers method design, code, analysis, figures, LaTeX, and self-review. Internal agent architecture, research memory, selection rules, and model-weight changes are not disclosed.

The projects were allocated 1,286 GPU-days from a 32-GPU pool, averaging about 38 GPU-days and 2.4 GPUs per project. The reported 0.38% human share measures messages, not labor time or scientific contribution.
ARR scores supply external feedback, but the release contains a summary report rather than all 34 papers, reviews, codebases, and protocols. All submissions were withdrawn after review.

The reported average score is 2.60 versus a historical human mean of 2.63; eight papers exceed 3.0 and two reach 3.67. Eleven predicted likely acceptances are estimates, not accepted papers. The value is a substantial automated-research trial whose project-level artifacts remain incompletely public.
ASI-Bench evaluates automated research execution across 60 projects in 11 fields under controlled information conditions.

The benchmark varies how much scientific guidance an agent receives: a full method, method context, only the goal and data, or distracting information. This separates following a supplied method from constructing one.
Tasks, required artifacts, and scoring stay fixed. Main experiments use isolated artifacts without external tools, so benchmark performance concerns execution within a specified research environment.
The study evaluates 18 agent/model configurations, usually with three runs; Opus 5 has one run. The design is not a complete factorial comparison of every agent and model.
Mean scores fall from 50.91 with full methods to 29.10 with method context and 26.62 with goals and data. The gap identifies dependence on scientific specification.
ASI-Bench is evaluation infrastructure for research agents. It does not itself demonstrate recursive updates to model parameters, research procedures, or inherited system state.
Recursive's First Steps reports automated AI-engineering results on NanoChat, NanoGPT, and GPU kernels.

The research produces concrete code improvements under task-specific evaluation. The public evidence concerns those artifacts rather than a complete, independently inspectable self-updating researcher.

NanoChat combines hashed bigram and trigram value embeddings with about 50 million dense parameters and a billion-entry sparse table. Search uses H100s; the final five-minute evaluation uses B200s across ten seeds.

NanoGPT targets FineWeb loss 3.28 on eight H100s: the blog reports 77.5 seconds, while the repository lists 77.3 seconds on Modal with official timing pending. SOL covers 235 kernels, of which ten are released.
The SOL score rises from 0.699 to 0.754, closing about 18% of the remaining score gap; that is not an 18% speedup. Human and AI work also harden the evaluator.

NanoChat averages 0.9109 BPB against a cleaned community result of 0.9372, with roughly 1.3 times faster attainment of the initial Karpathy baseline's quality. Results depend on the stated hardware, time limits, and evaluation revisions.
Hermes Agent is a persistent agent system that stores user facts, memory, procedures, and searchable session history outside model weights.

Different memory forms serve different purposes: compact always-present facts, progressively loaded skills, and retrieved historical detail. Persistence can improve continuity without changing the underlying model.

MEMORY has a 2,200-character budget and USER a 1,375-character budget. A frozen prompt snapshot keeps memory updates out of the current cached prompt; files change immediately. Oversized writes fail and require explicit cleanup.

Memory CRUD, skill loading, and FTS5 session search are public implementation features. Background review runs after the main turn using the main or an auxiliary model, with restricted memory, skill, and file-reading tools and optional human review.
Retained state is available to later sessions. The public code and documentation explain the mechanism, but each memory update does not undergo an independent held-out performance test.
The system is an inspectable example of external memory and skill maintenance. Its product capabilities do not by themselves quantify long-term capability gains or parameter-level learning.
INTELLECT-3 trains a 106B-total, 12B-active mixture-of-experts model from GLM-4.5-Air-Base through supervised and reinforcement-learning stages.
An engineered asynchronous training system supports large-scale reasoning and agent learning. The evolving object is the model; the training engine is not shown autonomously rewriting itself.
General and agent SFT use a fixed DeepSeek-R1 teacher. RL combines group-centered rewards, token importance-ratio masking, and Muon, with code tests, answer checks, and a fixed 7B checker.
AIME rises from 82 to 88, LiveCodeBench from 61.5 to 69.3, and GPQA from 73.3 to 74.4. AIME averages pass@1 over 32 samples; it is not best-of-32 accuracy.

The reported setup uses 60 nodes and 480 H200s: 16 nodes for training and 44 for sampling, 65,000-token context, and roughly 1,500-second steps. Mid-rollout weight updates improve throughput by more than twofold.

The 512-GPU, two-month figure covers the broader program, not RL alone. A hub containing 500 environments does not mean all were used for this run. The result is large-scale model training and infrastructure, with a fixed improvement procedure.
Intology Locus reports long-running AI research and post-training experiments through company previews of a private research stack.

The experiments test sustained execution and targeted optimization. Post-training results use benchmark-selected Qwen3-1.7B-Base checkpoints; the composite does not describe one general-purpose checkpoint.

Basic runs use ten hours on one H100. Extended post-training allocates about 4,500 H100-hours across seven tasks, with a 100-hour wall-clock limit or a stop after 50 evaluations without improvement. Each reported cell has one trial.

For AIME, eight H100s generate 3.17 billion tokens before filtering to at most 6,000 examples, reaching 3.64 billion total tokens. The system diagnoses nonterminating reasoning and rolls back changes.
Reported results include RE-Bench 1.30 at 64 hours versus human 1.27, MLE-Bench Lite 77% medals over 22 tasks, and post-training 44.7 or 51.6 extended versus an official 49.4 comparison.

These are company-reported, author-checked results from a private system; code may change after a recorded checkpoint. They demonstrate research outcomes under disclosed task budgets, with limited visibility into the researcher's inherited update mechanism.
Autoscience Lab develops automated AI scientists and engineers, with public descriptions of systems such as Carl and Mira.

The relevant ambition is end-to-end scientific and engineering work. Public milestones identify research directions and outputs, while the mechanism of researcher improvement needs separate technical evidence.
The reviewed materials describe external machine-learning solutions but do not disclose a complete model of research memory, candidate selection, or updates to the research system itself.

Company materials report an ICLR 2025 workshop contribution and a silver medal in Kaggle's Santa 2025 competition, which had roughly 3,300 teams. Complete Carl and Mira technical materials were not obtained in the recorded review.
The public record therefore supports an industry research entry and specific reported milestones. Funding and the number of deployed agents do not measure scientific quality or inherited learning.

A March 2026 release expands the company account, but the atlas retains the distinction between published outcomes and undisclosed internal mechanisms. No continuous recursive-improvement result can be reconstructed from the reviewed materials alone.
Reflexion improves task attempts through verbal reflection stored outside frozen model weights.
An agent can turn failure feedback into advice for its next attempt. The paper's verbal reinforcement-learning terminology describes this text-memory loop rather than gradient-based RL.
A fixed actor, evaluator, and self-reflection component maintain the latest one to three memory entries. Feedback may come from environment rewards or internal tests.

ALFWorld solves 130 of 134 tasks cumulatively within up to 12 trials. HumanEval rises from 80.1 to 91, while MBPP falls from 80.1 to 77.1. Internal testing allows up to six cycles, so the reported pass@1 result is not one model call.
For Rust, the full method scores 68, compared with 60 without reflection and 52 without tests. WebShop does not improve, showing that the usefulness of verbal feedback is task-dependent.

The inherited state is usually task-local reflective memory. These results motivate external experience loops, while offering no evidence that the improver or its model parameters recursively upgrade.
ReasoningBank stores generalizable reasoning lessons extracted from both successful and failed task trajectories while keeping the model frozen.
Failure contains reusable information when abstracted into a lesson rather than copied as an unsuccessful action sequence. Memory selection is as important as memory volume.
Up to three memory items are stored per task in JSON; embedding retrieval returns one by default. MaTTS compares multiple trajectories to support richer abstraction and test-time scaling.

Experiments cover 684 WebArena tasks, 1,341 Mind2Web tasks, and 500 SWE-bench tasks. Gemini Pro improves from 46.7 to 53.9 on WebArena and from 54 to 57.4 on SWE-bench; parallel MaTTS with five trajectories reaches 56.3 WebArena pass@1.
On shopping tasks, success-only memory scores 46.5 versus 49.7 with both successes and failures. Retrieving four items reduces performance to 44.4, illustrating the cost of irrelevant context.

Reported token use including reflection rises from 50,847.4 to 53,054.5. The result is an external-memory learning mechanism whose effectiveness depends on abstraction, retrieval, and inference budget.
HASE jointly trains a model to solve tasks and edit parts of its guidance and evaluation runtime, with an immutable oracle anchoring correctness.
A model can learn to improve the environment through which it acts, but editable evaluation must remain connected to an independent outcome criterion.
The same Qwen3-8B performs task solving and harness edits under GRPO. Patches are local to a rollout and pass staged validation; the commit controller stays fixed.

On S2D, the split is 200 training, 50 validation, and 212 test examples. HASE reports 86.98 ± 0.38 versus 86.8 for MetaHarness with a 120B model. The five repetitions are evaluation runs, not five independent training seeds.
For Heilbronn, fixed-weight performance is 0.021880 and joint training reaches 0.036082. Circle packing repairs two evaluator vulnerabilities and finishes at 2.635983.

The trained model is 8B, not the 120B comparison model. Counterexample consistency helps check edits but is not a proof of full evaluator correctness; the experiment supports bounded model–harness joint learning under a fixed oracle and commit procedure.

h-instructions.title: Instructions & Context Programs
h-instructions.question: How can a frozen model receive better instructions and context?
h-instructions.definition: Editable system and module prompts, demonstrations, context assembly, compression, and executable specifications shape conditional generation and tool use.

h-memory.title: Persistent Memory & Knowledge
h-memory.question: Which experience should persist, and how should it be retrieved and revised?
h-memory.definition: Episodic traces, rules, indexes, knowledge bases, and utility estimates store mutable state outside model weights. Their value depends on their use in later decisions.

h-capabilities.title: Tools, Skills & Action Interfaces
h-capabilities.question: How can interaction become callable and composable capability?
h-capabilities.definition: Tools, executable skills, descriptions, input/output contracts, and discovery interfaces can change. Skills, plugins, and MCP expose capabilities through different packaging and protocols.
subtopics: Plugins, skills, MCP, and calling protocols

h-control.title: Control Flow & Agent Architecture
h-control.question: When should agents plan, act, reflect, delegate, or stop?
h-control.definition: Control and information flow define roles, model routing, stopping, retries, loops, and dynamically generated subtasks. Graphs and code provide different representations.

h-runtime.title: Runtime, Environment & Infrastructure
h-runtime.question: How can the same model execute more effectively at lower cost?
h-runtime.definition: Persistent processes, REPL state, dependencies, scheduling, caches, context budgets, recovery, and deployment configuration determine how an agent runs. The agent runtime and its external task environment have distinct roles.

h-experience.title: Task Streams, Exploration & Curriculum
h-experience.question: Which next task provides useful results and useful learning signals?
h-experience.definition: Task selection determines which successes and failures become observable. Curricula, exploration, failure discovery, and transfer-task selection shape the experience distribution.

h-evaluation.title: Evaluation, Verifiers & Feedback
h-evaluation.question: How can system versions be compared when feedback or evaluators change?
h-evaluation.definition: Executable tests, environment rewards, human assessments, and model judgments guide updates and selection. Editable evaluators need a reliable connection to task outcomes.

h-search.title: Search, Selection & Evolution
h-search.question: How can expensive program search preserve useful intermediate discoveries?
h-search.definition: Reflection proposes directions, search allocates exploration, and selection determines inheritance. Populations and archives can preserve stepping stones that are not currently best.

h-improver.title: Self-Modification of the Improver
h-improver.question: Does an updated system change how the next improvement is produced?
h-improver.definition: Locate editable diagnosis, proposal, implementation, and research procedures. Check that successors execute the revised procedure, and identify which parent-selection, evaluation, and budget rules remain fixed.

h-inheritance.title: Inheritance, Composition & Transfer
h-inheritance.question: How does a change become reusable capability beyond its original task?
h-inheritance.definition: Prompts, memories, skills, program versions, and search experience can persist. Within-task reuse, task transfer, model transfer, and improver transfer are distinct outcomes.

m-bootstrapping.title: Self-training & bootstrapping
m-bootstrapping.question: Which model outputs should become the next training set?
m-bootstrapping.definition: Generated answers, rationales, and demonstrations return to parameter learning after selection. Quality, coverage, diversity, and regeneration by later checkpoints determine the loop.

m-preferences.title: Self-critique & AI feedback
m-preferences.question: How can critiques and comparisons become learning signals?
m-preferences.definition: Models produce critiques, revisions, and preferences from principles or rubrics. The judge may remain fixed or learn alongside the answering policy.
mechanisms: Preference pairs for DPO or reward-model RL

m-verifiable-feedback.title: Verifiable feedback & policy improvement
m-verifiable-feedback.question: Which outcomes provide scalable, grounded learning signals?
m-verifiable-feedback.definition: Answer checks, program execution, environment state, and formal proof checking can filter demonstrations or directly reward a policy. The feedback source is distinct from the optimizer.
mechanisms: Sample or search, execute, verify, update

m-evaluator-learning.title: Evaluator learning & generator–verifier co-training
m-evaluator-learning.question: How can evaluators detect errors made by stronger generators?
m-evaluator-learning.definition: Judges, reward models, and verifiers learn from new difficult examples and then influence generation or data selection. Shared and separate weights support different implementations.

m-self-play.title: Task generation & self-play
m-self-play.question: How can a model continually encounter learnable challenges?
m-self-play.definition: Proposers, challengers, or opponents respond to solver performance by changing tasks or opposition. Task generation differs from selection from a fixed pool.
mechanisms: Solver feedback, task generation, solver learning

m-curriculum-learning.title: Adaptive curriculum & data selection
m-curriculum-learning.question: Where should a limited training budget be spent?
m-curriculum-learning.definition: A curriculum controller changes sampling using difficulty, expected learning value, or measured improvement. A hard or rare example is not necessarily a useful training example.
mechanisms: Learner feedback, sampling weights, training, reevaluation

m-experience-learning.title: Interactive learning & experience reuse
m-experience-learning.question: How do multi-step interactions become transferable policy skills?
m-experience-learning.definition: Tool, web, game, and code trajectories train action policies through rewards, credit assignment, selected demonstrations, and replay. External-memory writes and weight updates are recorded separately.

m-learned-updates.title: Learning to adapt & learned improvement policies
m-learned-updates.question: How can a system learn which changes improve a learner?
m-learned-updates.definition: An inner loop performs data learning, reward learning, skill maintenance, or harness editing. An outer objective trains the improvement policy from performance after that change.

m-continual-adaptation.title: Continual learning & test-time adaptation
m-continual-adaptation.question: When should deployment experience change persistent parameters?
m-continual-adaptation.definition: Specify which parameters change, when adaptation occurs, what resets, and how previous knowledge persists. Continual adaptation can use SFT, RL, self-play, or other learning mechanisms.

m-pretraining-ai4ai.title: AI-assisted pretraining
m-pretraining-ai4ai.question: How can AI improve pretraining data and algorithms?
m-pretraining-ai4ai.definition: AI may rewrite corpora, select mixtures, design objectives or optimizers, and improve training code. A self-improvement loop additionally feeds training outcomes back into those AI components.

x-workflow.title: Workflow–Policy Co-adaptation
x-workflow.question: How should models and execution workflows adapt to each other?
x-workflow.definition: A workflow changes the state and action distribution a model encounters. Updating the model can then change which workflow is effective.

x-internalization.title: Harness-to-Model Internalization
x-internalization.question: Which external capabilities can survive removal of their support?
x-internalization.definition: Traces and signals from tools, workflows, skills, or teacher interventions enter weights through SFT, RL, or distillation. Deployment tests establish which capabilities persist.

x-externalization.title: Model-to-Harness Design
x-externalization.question: Can better model behavior produce better system designs?
x-externalization.definition: A model proposes tools, workflows, environments, or training changes. Selected modifications alter later execution and learning; design ability is measured separately from task-solving ability.

x-memory.title: Skill–Memory–Policy Co-evolution
x-memory.question: How do changing skills and the policy using them learn together?
x-memory.definition: External skills or memory operations are added, revised, and removed while the policy or controller learns to use them. Content updates and usage-policy updates have separate effects.
subtopics: Memory write, update, and delete policies

x-environment.title: Environment–Curriculum Co-adaptation
x-environment.question: How do tasks and interfaces respond to the learner?
x-environment.definition: Policy performance changes task generation, difficulty, or environment wrappers, which reshape experience. A learned world model provides simulated experience through a different update object.

x-feedback.title: Reward–Evaluator–Policy Coupling
x-feedback.question: How do changing policies and evaluators shape each other's data?
x-feedback.definition: Policy trajectories provide evaluator training or diagnostic evidence. Evaluations then determine selection and parameter updates. Weight-based reward models and tool-based evaluators use distinct representations.

x-training.title: Training-Harness Co-evolution
x-training.question: Can training results improve the system that runs training?
x-training.definition: Results guide edits to training code, data processing, reward recipes, diagnostics, and research memory. Specify which parts of the research system persist and change.

x-organization.title: Organization–Policy Co-learning
x-organization.question: How should roles and communication change with learned capabilities?
x-organization.definition: Roles, communication, routing, and allocation organize execution; parameter updates change what each role can do. Co-learning concerns their interaction.

x-deployment.title: Deployment-time Re-adaptation
x-deployment.question: How should systems recover from changing models and interfaces?
x-deployment.definition: Model and harness updates occur on different schedules. Training may cover interface variation, while deployment feedback triggers later learning or system edits.

harness.title: Harness
harness.tagline: Learning through persistent state and executable systems
harness.definition: The main update objects are prompts, memory, skills, tools, control flow, runtime code, and improvement procedures outside foundation-model weights.
harness.question: Which edits improve both task performance and the ability to produce later improvements?
harness.scene: An agent runs tasks, records outcomes and failures, proposes edits, evaluates candidates, and retains useful versions. The recursive case also places parts of the improvement procedure inside the editable system.
open_questions: Which skills and edits transfer across tasks, models, and environments?
When does better task performance improve the ability to discover the next useful change?
How can changing evaluators and task streams preserve meaningful comparisons?

model.title: Model
model.tagline: Learning through parameter updates and renewed feedback
model.definition: Self-generated data, critiques, verification, curricula, interaction, and learned update policies change model parameters. Track the actual trained model separately from fixed teachers and judges.
model.question: How can generated experience continue to supply useful learning signals while preserving transfer and existing capabilities?
model.scene: A checkpoint generates or selects experience, receives feedback, and undergoes a parameter update. Later checkpoints reshape the data, tasks, or evaluations used for subsequent learning.
open_questions: What supplies new information when successive models share errors?
How can evaluators and curricula keep pace with the learner?
Which gains transfer and persist after repeated updates?

hybrid.title: Model × Harness
hybrid.tagline: Learning across weights and the systems around them
hybrid.definition: Parameters include policies, evaluators, world models, and controllers. External state includes workflows, tools, skills, memory, environment wrappers, and training programs. Identify the updates and feedback on both sides.
hybrid.question: When do sequential adaptation and two-way feedback become sustained coevolution?
hybrid.scene: An external system shapes trajectories used to train the model. The updated model changes which system designs work and may help create the next design. Cross-combination experiments separate model gains, harness gains, and their interaction.
open_questions: Which external capabilities can be internalized without losing reliability?
Does stronger task-solving ability improve system-design ability?
How should updates be scheduled when models, interfaces, and evaluators change together?

rel-002.explanation: DGM explicitly compares with ADAS's fixed meta-agent and includes a fixed-seed modifier ablation.

rel-003.explanation: DGM discusses SICA as related contemporaneous work, distinguishing archives and branching exploration; this is not a code-inheritance claim.

rel-004.explanation: HGM compares with DGM and allocates search using descendant value; comparison alone does not establish implementation inheritance.

rel-005.explanation: AFlow discusses and evaluates against ADAS, changing how search trials are allocated in workflow space.

rel-006.explanation: ACE uses GEPA as a baseline to compare prompt evolution with incremental maintenance of contextual experience.

rel-007.explanation: Meta-Harness compares with ACE in online classification while searching executable information-access code.

rel-008.explanation: Iterative RPO describes itself as a simplified self-rewarding instance using fixed questions, correct-answer scoring, and positive-response NLL.

rel-009.explanation: Iterative RPO contrasts preference learning from positive and negative samples with STaR's SFT on selected reasoning.

rel-010.explanation: Self-Taught Evaluators identifies self-rewarding preference training as an application; this does not establish a jointly executed system.

rel-011.explanation: The Salesforce study uses GEPA-style failure-driven harness edits before adapting student weights.

rel-012.explanation: DGM discusses the Gödel Machine and replaces proof of net benefit with empirical task evaluation.

rel-014.explanation: STOP evaluates an improver through the utility of its outputs; SICA lets the current coding agent edit its own implementation.

rel-015.explanation: HyperAgents makes the meta-agent editable; AIDE² keeps the main outer loop fixed and separately tests successor-led research.

rel-016.explanation: Both search prompts: GEPA emphasizes trajectory reflection and Pareto complementarity, while Promptbreeder coevolves mutation prompts.

rel-017.explanation: ACE maintains experience content; MemRL learns memory utility from rewards. Both can freeze the foundation model.

rel-018.explanation: Voyager accumulates Minecraft code skills; SkillWeaver packages web interaction into APIs. Both study composable capabilities from experience.

rel-019.explanation: Voyager reuses executable behavior, whereas ACE retains a textual playbook for later decisions.

rel-020.explanation: RRSI constrains specialization and cost during proposal and acceptance; ModularRSI organizes transferable edits through modular search and integration.

rel-021.explanation: SOL-π emphasizes runtime efficiency; AIDE² directly optimizes research agents. Whether cheaper execution improves successor research requires a separate test.

rel-022.explanation: One study separates improver and executor; the other compares spending the same resources on harness edits or direct task solving.

rel-023.explanation: LLMs Can Self-Improve mainly filters by answer consistency; ReST-EM uses external binary feedback and repeated self-training.

rel-024.explanation: Both regenerate training data: ReST-EM learns selected successes, while Iterative RPO combines preference pairs and positive NLL.

rel-025.explanation: Both learn evaluation: Self-Taught Evaluators trains preference judgment; DeepSeekMath-V2 iterates proof verification and generation.

rel-026.explanation: DeepSeekMath-V2 uses proof verification and meta-verification; Kimi K2 calibrates a critic with verifiable trajectories before open-task feedback.

rel-027.explanation: Self-Rewarding LMs construct preferences and apply DPO by rounds; Kimi K2 updates actor–critic feedback within RL.

rel-028.explanation: Dr. Zero generates search questions and uses retrieval; SIMA 2 uses an external Gemini task generator and evaluator whose weights are not co-trained.

rel-029.explanation: GPT-Red couples attack and defense through competition; the mathematical system couples generation and verification through complementary roles.

rel-030.explanation: SEAL learns self-edits or learning data; DERL learns reward programs. Both evaluate a design through its effect on a downstream learner.

rel-031.explanation: MASS alternates workflow evolution and shared-model training; the Salesforce study addresses teacher–student mismatch with corrections on student-visited states.

rel-032.explanation: Both alternate external-system and weight updates. MASS emphasizes shared multi-role weights; Co-Harness diagnoses failures and revises runtime mechanisms.

rel-033.explanation: Both address student-visited states. On-policy harness coevolution retains the optimized harness; Harness-Zero converts stronger-harness guidance into target-action supervision and removes the teacher harness at deployment.

rel-034.explanation: EvoTrainer edits training procedures, signals, and skills; Co-Harness first edits the runtime that generates learning trajectories.

rel-035.explanation: SkillRL combines skills with execution and RL; Skill Self-Play also uses skills to structure task generation and verification.
